questions.question: foldr :: (a -> b -> b) -> b -> [a] -> b. What are the three arguments, in order?
options: A combining function, a starting value, and the list to fold
The list, a starting value, and a combining function
Two lists and a combining function
A starting value, the list, and a combining function
questions.explanation: Reading the type left to right: the first argument is (a -> b -> b), a function combining one element with an already-folded result; the second, plain b, is the starting value used once the list runs out; the third, [a], is the list being folded.
optionFeedback: Correct — combining function first, then the base value, then the list, matching the order the type lists them in.
The list is always foldr's last argument, not its first — this order would not match the type (a -> b -> b) -> b -> [a] -> b.
foldr folds one list, not two — its inputs are a function, a base value, and a single list.
The combining function comes first in the type, not last — swapping it to the end does not match (a -> b -> b) -> b -> [a] -> b.

questions.question: Why does foldr (:) [] [1,2,3] return [1,2,3] unchanged?
options: Because foldr's substitution rule replaces every : with the combining function and [] with the starting value — and here both are already (:) and [], so nothing changes
Because foldr always returns its list argument unchanged, regardless of the combining function
Because (:) is a special case foldr recognises and short-circuits on
Because [] as a starting value always means 'return the input list as-is'
questions.explanation: foldr f acc [1,2,3] is the substitution picture 1 `f` (2 `f` (3 `f` acc)). With f = (:) and acc = [], that becomes 1 : (2 : (3 : [])) — which is just [1,2,3] written out in full, so the 'substitution' happens to reconstruct exactly what was there.
optionFeedback: Correct — replacing : with (:) and [] with [] is a substitution that changes nothing, since those are already the list's own constructors.
foldr can absolutely change its input — foldr (+) 0 [1,2,3] returns 6, not [1,2,3]; the identity here is specific to choosing (:) and [] as the arguments.
foldr treats (:) as an ordinary two-argument function, exactly like (+) or max — there is no special-casing.
The starting value only matters once the list is exhausted; [] here is simply what [] gets replaced with by the substitution, not a general 'return input unchanged' signal.

questions.question: Trace foldr max 0 [3,9,2] using the substitution picture. What does it produce?
options: max 3 (max 9 (max 2 0)) = 9
max 0 (max 2 (max 9 3)) = 9
max(3,9,2) treated as a three-argument call = error
max 3 (max 9 (max 2 0)) = 3
questions.explanation: Substituting : with max and [] with 0 on 3 : (9 : (2 : [])) gives max 3 (max 9 (max 2 0)). Innermost first: max 2 0 = 2, then max 9 2 = 9, then max 3 9 = 9.
optionFeedback: Correct — working from the innermost combination outward: max 2 0 = 2, max 9 2 = 9, max 3 9 = 9.
This reverses the nesting direction — foldr nests toward the right starting from the first element, giving max 3 (max 9 (max 2 0)), not this order.
max is a two-argument curried function throughout; foldr always applies it to exactly two arguments at a time, never three at once.
The nesting and nearly the whole computation are right, but the outermost combination is max 3 9, which is 9, not 3.

questions.question: length' = foldr (\_ n -> n + 1) 0. What does the combining function do with each element?
options: It ignores the element entirely (matched by the wildcard _) and just adds one to the running count
It adds the element's value to n
It replaces n with the element itself
It multiplies n by the element
questions.explanation: \_ n -> n + 1 discards whatever element foldr hands it — the wildcard _ never binds it to a name — and adds one to the accumulator regardless of the element's value, which is exactly how you count elements without caring what they are.
optionFeedback: Correct — the wildcard _ means the element itself is never used; only n, the running count, is incremented.
The element's value never appears on the right-hand side of the lambda at all — only n is read, and only n + 1 is computed.
n is incremented, not replaced — each step adds one to whatever count has been accumulated so far.
There is no multiplication in this combining function, and the element's value is never even bound to a name.

questions.question: map' f = foldr (\x acc -> f x : acc) []. Why does this definition show that foldr is 'the general shape of list recursion'?
options: Because map's own behaviour — apply f to the head, then cons it onto the recursive result on the tail — is exactly what foldr's combining function does at each step, with [] supplying map's own base case
Because foldr and map always produce identical-looking code with no differences
Because map' is faster than the ordinary map
Because foldr can only be used to define map, never filter
questions.explanation: map f (x:xs) = f x : map f xs is exactly f x : acc with acc playing the role of the recursive call, and map f [] = [] is exactly foldr's base value []. filter' right below it shows the same shape works for filter too, which is the actual point: foldr is general enough to express both.
optionFeedback: Correct — map's own two equations line up directly with foldr's combining function and base value.
The two definitions look different (map' uses foldr explicitly; ordinary map does not) — what matches is their behaviour, not their surface code.
Nothing here is about performance; you would not normally write map this way precisely because the direct recursive definition is clearer, not faster.
filter' p = foldr (\x acc -> if p x then x : acc else acc) [] is defined the very same way, right alongside map' — foldr expresses both.

questions.question: and' = foldr (&&) True. Why must (&&) be parenthesised here?
options: A bare operator like && is not a valid expression on its own; parentheses turn it into an ordinary function value that can be passed as an argument
&& requires parentheses only when combined specifically with True
Without parentheses, && would be interpreted as two separate Booleans
foldr requires every one of its arguments to be wrapped in parentheses, regardless of what they are
questions.explanation: This is the same rule from Currying and Sections: an operator written bare is a parse error, not a value. (&&) converts the operator into a curried function &&'s own type, Bool -> Bool -> Bool, which is exactly the (a -> b -> b) shape foldr's first argument needs.
optionFeedback: Correct — the reason is general (bare operators are never valid expressions), not specific to pairing && with True.
The issue has nothing to do with what the second argument is; a bare && would fail to parse as an argument regardless of what followed it.
&& is a single operator token; it is not read as two separate values either way, parenthesised or not.
foldr's other arguments (a starting value, a list) are ordinary values or lists and need no such parentheses — only a bare operator being passed as a value needs them.

questions.question: foldr (-) 0 [1,2,3] is 2, but foldl (-) 0 [1,2,3] is -6. What causes the difference?
options: - is not associative, so grouping from the right ((1 - (2 - 3)) vs. grouping from the left (((0-1)-2)-3) gives different answers
foldl has a bug and should be avoided entirely
foldr and foldl use different starting values even when given the same 0
The list [1,2,3] is processed in a different order of elements by each fold, not just a different grouping
questions.explanation: Both folds visit the elements 1, 2, 3 in the same order — the difference is purely how the combining calls are nested. foldr gives 1 - (2 - (3 - 0)) = 2; foldl gives ((0 - 1) - 2) - 3 = -6. Because subtraction is not associative, these two groupings produce different results.
optionFeedback: Correct — same elements, same operator, different grouping, and subtraction is sensitive to grouping.
Both folds are correctly implemented; the difference is an inherent property of using a non-associative operator, not a defect.
Both start from the same 0 — the starting value is not where the two folds diverge.
Both process 1, then 2, then 3 in the same left-to-right order over the list; what differs is which combination happens innermost first.

questions.question: take 3 (foldr (:) [] [1..]) returns [1,2,3], but the foldl equivalent never returns. Why?
options: foldl must consume the entire list to build its final accumulator before returning anything, and [1..] never ends; foldr can produce its first result immediately
foldl is simply slower than foldr on every list, finite or not
[1..] is not a valid Haskell list, so only foldr can process it
take 3 only works correctly with foldr, never with foldl, regardless of the list
questions.explanation: foldr (:) [] [1..] can hand back 1 : (foldr (:) [] [2..]) without evaluating the rest, so take 3 only forces the three cons cells it needs. foldl has no partial result to offer until it has walked the whole list — which, for [1..], is a walk that never ends.
optionFeedback: Correct — the issue is not raw speed but whether a fold can produce a usable partial result before reaching the end of the list.
On a finite list both folds terminate; foldl is not inherently 'slower', it simply cannot start producing output before finishing the whole traversal.
[1..] is a perfectly ordinary (infinite) Haskell list — plenty of Prelude functions, including foldr with a lazy combining function, can work with it.
take 3 works fine with foldl too, as long as the list is finite — the problem here is specific to combining take with foldl on an infinite list.

questions.question: ((*2) . (+1)) 5 — which computation runs first, and what is the final result?
options: (+1) runs first (5 + 1 = 6), then (*2) doubles it to 12
(*2) runs first (5 * 2 = 10), then (+1) adds one to get 11
Both run simultaneously and the results are added: 6 + 10 = 16
Composition is left to right here, so (*2) applies to 5 first
questions.explanation: (f . g) x = f (g x), so f . g applies g first, then f. Here f = (*2) and g = (+1), so (+1) runs on 5 first, giving 6, and then (*2) doubles it to 12.
optionFeedback: Correct — the right-hand function in a composition runs first, matching (f . g) x = f (g x).
This is the order for g . f, not f . g — here (*2) is the left-hand (outer) function, so it runs last, not first.
Composition is sequential, not simultaneous — one function's result feeds directly into the other as its argument, not added together.
Composition is read right to left: (.) always applies its right-hand argument first, regardless of which function is written where.

questions.question: sumOddSquares = sum . map (^2) . filter odd. Reading right to left, what is the second stage?
options: map (^2), squaring the odd numbers that survived filter odd
filter odd, since composition still evaluates left to right in practice
sum, because it is applied to the whole pipeline's final result
There is no meaningful order — all three run at once
questions.explanation: Reading right to left: filter odd runs first, keeping only odd elements; map (^2) runs second, squaring what survived; sum runs last, adding everything up. So the second stage is map (^2).
optionFeedback: Correct — filter odd is first (rightmost), map (^2) is second, and sum is last (leftmost).
Composition genuinely evaluates right to left, both in the substitution rule (f . g) x = f (g x) and in what actually happens when the pipeline runs.
sum is applied last, to whatever map (^2) . filter odd produced — it is the third and final stage, not the second.
Each stage's output is the next stage's input, so they cannot run at once — the pipeline is inherently sequential.

questions.question: sum $ map (^2) $ filter odd [1..10] and sum (map (^2) (filter odd [1..10])) — how do these two expressions relate?
options: They compute the same thing; $ just applies a function to an argument with the lowest possible precedence, removing the need for nested parentheses
$ changes the order of evaluation compared to ordinary parentheses
$ is only valid with sum, not with arbitrary functions
The version using $ is evaluated lazily while the parenthesised version is evaluated strictly
questions.explanation: ($) :: (a -> b) -> a -> b with f $ x = f x. Because $ has the lowest possible precedence, everything to its right is grouped together before the function on its left is applied — which is exactly what nested parentheses achieve, just without writing them out.
optionFeedback: Correct — $ is ordinary function application spelled with lower precedence; it does not change what gets computed or when.
$ does not reorder evaluation; it only changes how the parentheses would otherwise have to be written, thanks to its very low precedence.
$ works with any function value on its left — sum is not special here.
Both expressions have identical evaluation behaviour under Haskell's laziness; $ is purely a parsing convenience, not an evaluation-strategy change.
